title: Computer Networks
summary: How the Internet works, layer by layer: from framing and error checks on a single link, through shared media, IP and routing, to TCP, applications such as DNS and email, and the security protocols that protect each layer. Two lectures a week follow the Tanenbaum, Feamster and Wetherall textbook (6th edition), with two self-study readings, seven tutorials and weekly WebLab assignments alongside. Much of the course is about running the core algorithms by hand on small examples.

basis.description: Slides of the 12 lectures of the 2024-25 edition, the chapter summaries, the two self-study notes (Error Detection and Correction, Cryptography) and the seven tutorials. Time shares count text slides; each self-study note is estimated as one average lecture (36 slides), since neither has lecture slides.
basis.caveat: From 2026-27 the course is CSE14B in year 1, quarter 4, renamed from CSE1405 with unchanged content. Error detection is taught only through self-study, so its share is an estimate; the security share also counts the cryptography notes as one lecture, and the Lecture 10 slides alone would give it less.

topics.name: Layers and network performance
know: The seven OSI layers in order, what each of physical, data link, network, transport and application does, and that session and presentation have hardly any protocols of their own
The name of the unit each layer sends: [[bit, frame, packet, segment]]
Which layers run on every router along a path and which run only on the two end hosts
How TCP/IP differs from OSI: [[physical and data link merged, no session or presentation layer]]
Connection-oriented versus connectionless service, and what state means in a protocol
Propagation delay, transmission delay, round-trip time, bandwidth, throughput and goodput, each defined precisely
do: Order the layers and place a protocol or device on the right one
Argue why layering helps: lower layers can be swapped without touching the ones above
Say what a single ping can and cannot tell you about route, delay and processing time
pitfalls: Confusing [[transmission delay (pushing all bits onto the wire)]] with [[propagation delay (one bit travelling to the other end)]]
Assuming reliability at the data link layer makes the end-to-end path reliable: routers can still drop packets

topics.name: Error detection and correction
know: Parity bits, even versus odd parity, and Hamming distance
Parity words and the Internet checksum: [[add the blocks, wrap the carry back in, take the 1's complement]]
CRC: [[append as many zeros as the generator has bits minus one, divide with XOR]], the remainder is the check value
Parity blocks with a row and a column of parity bits, and how they locate and fix a single flipped bit
Hamming codes: [[parity bits at positions 1, 2, 4, 8]] and so on counted from the left, each covering the positions whose binary index contains it
How many parity bits m data bits need, so that you can give the length of an (n, m) code
Burst errors and why they shape the choice of detection method
do: Compute an Internet checksum for 4-bit blocks
Compute the CRC to send, check a received CRC, or work out which generators could have produced it
Fill in the parity bits of a parity block, or find the flipped bit in a received one
Encode a message with an (11,7), (19,14) or (21,16) Hamming code, with even or odd parity as asked
pitfalls: Using even parity when the question asks for odd, or the other way round: the rubric gives only half the points
Writing just the codeword: full points need the parity positions and how each bit was filled
Forgetting to add the overflow back in before taking the 1's complement of a checksum

topics.name: Reliable links: sliding windows and framing
know: Stop-and-wait with ARQ, timeouts, sequence numbers and piggybacked acknowledgements
Sliding window with window size k, and how k limits throughput when the first ACK comes back late
Go-back-N versus selective repeat: receiver buffer, what is resent, and when each is the better choice
Cumulative and duplicate acknowledgements, and negative acknowledgements
Framing by byte count, byte stuffing with FLAG and ESC bytes, and [[bit stuffing after five 1s]]
Frame structure: [[header, payload, trailer]]
do: Compute throughput and goodput of a sliding window link from frame size, header share, bandwidth, k and the latency in each direction
Work backwards from a given goodput to the header fraction or another unknown
Trace selective repeat with an error and timeouts to find which frames are resent
Byte-stuff or unstuff a frame, and give the worst-case size after stuffing
pitfalls: Not checking whether k frames are sent before the first ACK returns; that comparison decides the throughput formula
Removing escaped data bytes when unstuffing: [[drop the FLAG at each end and the ESC bytes, keep what was escaped]]

topics.name: MAC sublayer, Ethernet, Wi-Fi and switches
know: ALOHA and slotted ALOHA, and why [[slots double the efficiency]]
1-persistent, nonpersistent and p-persistent CSMA, and collision-free protocols: token ring, bit-map, binary countdown
CSMA/CD, the [[2 tau collision detection time]] and why Ethernet needs a minimum frame size
Binary exponential backoff: after collision i, [[wait a random number of slots from 0 to 2 to the power i, minus 1]]
Hidden and exposed terminals, MACA with RTS and CTS, and CSMA/CA in 802.11 with NAV, paused backoff and stop-and-wait ACKs
802.11 infrastructure and ad-hoc mode, and why a frame can carry three or four addresses
Hubs versus switches, backward learning, and the Spanning Tree Protocol with [[the smallest ID as root]]
do: Trace a CSMA/CA timeline with several stations, backoffs and ACKs to find when a station may send
Compute backoff ranges or the probability of a given number of collisions on Ethernet
Decide which stations can send in a MACA scenario with given ranges
Fill in a switch table from a sequence of frames, and draw the spanning tree of a switch network
pitfalls: In CSMA/CA, restarting a backoff that was paused instead of resuming it where it stopped
In a switch table, keeping an old port for an address that has since been seen on a new port

topics.name: Network layer: IP, fragmentation and helpers
know: Internet structure: hosts, routers, autonomous systems and Internet exchange points
IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, their sizes and notation, including shortening IPv6 addresses
The key IPv4 header fields (addresses, TTL, checksum, fragment fields) and what IPv6 changed
Transparent and nontransparent fragmentation and MTU discovery; [[IPv6 uses only MTU discovery]]
DHCP, ICMP and traceroute, ARP, and NAT mapping [[internal address plus port to an external port]]
Network-layer congestion control: provisioning, traffic-aware routing, throttling, ECN and RED
do: Count the fragments arriving at each network with and without MTU discovery
Say when the IP checksum and the TCP checksum of a fragmented segment can each be checked
Explain how NAT rewrites outgoing and incoming packets, and convert a prefix length to a subnet mask
pitfalls: Fragmenting the whole packet at once by the smallest MTU when there is no MTU discovery: [[each router splits the fragments it receives]]
Describing NAT without ports: the rubric gives most points only for the internal address and port to external port mapping

topics.name: Routing and IP prefixes
know: Forwarding versus routing, and what a routing table holds: [[destination, cost and outgoing line]]
Distance vector routing and the count-to-infinity problem
Link state routing: flooding link state packets and computing shortest paths
IP prefixes, CIDR and [[longest prefix match]]
Intra-domain routing ([[OSPF, link state]]) versus inter-domain routing ([[BGP, path vector]])
do: Build a router's table from its neighbours' distance vectors and the link costs, using the stated tie-break
Compute shortest-path costs and first hops from a weighted graph
Pick the prefix that handles a given destination address
pitfalls: Writing the full path where the table asks for the outgoing line: the rubric deducts points for it
Ignoring the tie-break rule the question gives for equal-cost options

topics.name: Transport layer: UDP and TCP
know: Ports, Berkeley socket primitives, and multiplexing versus inverse multiplexing
UDP: the [[8-byte header]] and why its checksum is optional
TCP header, three-way handshake, and which flags use up a sequence number ([[SYN and FIN do, a bare ACK does not]])
[[Sequence and acknowledgement numbers count bytes]]; duplicate ACKs and fast retransmission
Clock-based initial sequence numbers, packet lifetime and the forbidden region
Symmetric and asymmetric connection release, and the two-armies problem
Flow control with the receiver window, silly-window syndrome, and congestion control: slow start, threshold, additive increase, TCP Tahoe and TCP Reno
Head-of-line blocking and how QUIC avoids it with independent streams over UDP
do: Compute the sequence or acknowledgement number of a later segment after a handshake
Compute when clock-based sequence numbers reach the forbidden region, or the number of sequence bits from that time
Trace a congestion window through slow start, additive increase and a congestion signal under Tahoe or Reno
pitfalls: Forgetting the 1 that the SYN adds to the initial sequence number
Mixing up [[Tahoe (window back to 1) and Reno (window set to the new threshold)]] after a congestion signal

topics.name: Network security and cryptography
know: [[Confidentiality, integrity and availability]]; authentication; repudiation versus nonrepudiation
Full, responsible and coordinated disclosure of vulnerabilities
Stream and block ciphers, S-boxes and P-boxes, and the modes ECB, CBC and counter mode
Textbook RSA ([[n = p times q, c to the power d mod n]]), hybrid encryption and Diffie-Hellman
MACs versus digital signatures, cryptographic hash properties, hash-then-sign, and PKIs
WEP and why it failed, WPA2 and WPA3; firewalls with signature- or anomaly-based detection, discard versus TCP reset
IPsec and VPNs in transport and tunnel mode, Tor onion routing and onion services, TLS, DNS spoofing and DNSSEC
PGP ([[sign, then encrypt with a fresh symmetric key]] sent under the receiver's public key) and OTR
do: Encrypt or decrypt a few 4-bit blocks with a given S-box or P-box in CBC or counter mode
Decrypt a small RSA ciphertext
Explain the steps of onion encryption, PGP or a responsible disclosure
Judge which security properties a system needs and which protocol provides them
pitfalls: Applying the P-box forwards when decrypting; the rubric halves the points for it
Doing XOR and S-box in the wrong order in CBC, or XOR-ing with the wrong block
Saying a relay uses its public key in Tor: the layers use [[the shared keys set up with each relay]]

topics.name: Application layer: DNS, email, web and P2P
know: DNS name space, name servers, resource records, recursive versus iterative lookups, and why DNS runs over UDP
Email: envelope, header and body; [[SMTP to send, IMAP or POP3 to read]]
Base64: [[three bytes become four 6-bit characters, with = padding]]
HTTP requests and status codes, URLs, persistent connections, pipelining versus multiplexing
Video streaming: I, P and B frames, buffering, interleaving, and live and interactive streaming
CDNs and DNS redirection, BitTorrent, Chord DHT finger tables, and the three kinds of blockchain
do: Encode bytes in Base64 or decode a Base64 string, including padding
Count the queries of an uncached DNS lookup, and say which server a CDN returns for a lookup
Fill in a Chord finger table: [[entry i is the successor of the node's position plus 2 to the power i, modulo the ring size]]
pitfalls: Getting the padding wrong at the end of a Base64 string
Forgetting that a CDN name server sees the address of whoever sends it the lookup, which in a recursive lookup is the local name server

prerequisites: Binary and hexadecimal numbers, XOR and modular arithmetic, from Computer Organisation and Reasoning and Logic
Logarithms and powers of two, for Hamming code lengths, sequence numbers and backoff
Basic probability for collision and backoff questions; Probability Theory and Statistics runs in the same quarter
Shortest paths in a weighted graph, from Algorithms and Data Structures
practical: Seven ungraded tutorials (error detection, error correction, sliding windows, network layer, two on transport and application, cryptography) and weekly WebLab programming or Wireshark assignments of 2 to 5 hours, done in the shared lab hours with TAs. Two self-study notes of 3 to 4 hours each, on error detection and correction and on cryptography, come before the matching tutorials. None of it counts towards the grade, but the tutorials are close to exam questions.
studyAdvice: Read the Error Detection and Correction notes in week 1: they come before Tutorials 1 and 2, and those calculations are 14 percent of the exam points with no lecture to catch up from.
Do the cryptography notes before Lecture 10. S-box and P-box encryption, RSA and the protocol questions together make security the largest topic on the papers.

Practise each calculation type until it is routine: checksum, CRC, Hamming code, sliding window goodput, fragmentation, distance vector table, TCP sequence numbers, forbidden region, Base64, Chord finger table, CBC or counter mode.
Work through all seven tutorials and check them against the posted solutions; the exam reuses their formats with new numbers.
Learn the delay and throughput definitions early. They are not asked as definitions, but the sliding window and forbidden region calculations depend on them.
For the MAC sublayer and Wi-Fi, draw timelines. Most questions there are scenarios: who hears whom, who backs off, when someone may send.
In the last week sit two or three past papers in 120 minutes and write out every step, as full points need the working.
